notes: NHS cross-border treatment appeal; ECJ reference deferred final outcome but Article 49/22 principles and Munby J declarations are fully analysed.

enrichment.short_title: NHS reimbursement for treatment abroad under EU law
key_facts: Mrs Watts, a 72-year-old NHS patient with severe bilateral hip arthritis, sought authorisation to have hip replacement surgery in France under Form E112 after facing long NHS waiting times.

Bedford PCT refused support in November 2002 and again in February 2003, treating her as a routine case within NHS Plan targets; she proceeded to have surgery in Abbeville in March 2003 at a cost of about £3,900.

Munby J granted declarations that NHS hospital treatment falls within Article 49 EC and that undue delay must be assessed individually, but dismissed her reimbursement claim on the facts as at February 2003.
The Secretary of State appealed the legal declarations and sought an ECJ reference; Mrs Watts cross-appealed on waiting-list relevance and the period of delay to be considered.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from judicial review of the Secretary of State's refusal to authorise NHS payment for treatment abroad.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal deferred pending reference to the Court of Justice; the court indicated it would refer questions on NHS obligations under Geraets-Smits and Müller-Fauré, reimbursement bases, and criteria for undue delay.
enrichment.ratio: The Court of Justice has already rejected the argument that Article 49 does not apply to a state-funded NHS; undue delay for authorising treatment abroad is a clinical necessity test and should not be determined solely by NHS waiting lists, though Article 22.2 is ambiguous and may not require regard to normal waiting times.
legal_issues: Whether the NHS constitutes provision of services under Article 49 EC
Whether NHS waiting times are relevant to undue delay under Article 49 or Article 22
Whether Article 22 and Article 49 impose the same delay test after Inizan
Basis and extent of reimbursement for treatment abroad
Whether an ECJ reference is necessary given the budgetary implications for the NHS
linked_authorities: Geraets-Smits v Stichting Ziekenfonds YGS [2002] QB 409
Müller-Fauré and Van Riet v Onderlinge Waarborgmaatschappij Case C-385/99
Inizan v Caisse primaire d'assurance maladie des Hauts-de-Seine Case C-56/01
Kohll v Union des Caisses de Maladie Case C-158/96
R v Cambridge Health Authority ex parte B [1995] 1 WLR 898

confidence.notes: Legal analysis and proposed ECJ questions are explicit. Final disposition of the appeal awaits the reference, but the core EU/NHS principles are clearly stated.

notes: First appellate guidance on travel restriction orders under section 33 CJPA 2001; 15-year order reduced to five years.

enrichment.short_title: Travel restriction order after cocaine importation
key_facts: Mr Mee pleaded guilty to importing 1.955 kg of pure cocaine concealed in fruit juice tins from Jamaica and was sentenced to seven years' imprisonment.
The judge also imposed a 15-year travel restriction order under section 33, to run from release, without explaining why that length was chosen.
The importation was deliberate and sophisticated: Mee had returned to Jamaica shortly before the offence, had contacts at both ends of the trade, and gave unsatisfactory accounts in interview.
Personal mitigation and good character pointed to a lower, though still significant, risk of reoffending through future travel.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against a travel restriction order imposed on sentence for a post-commencement drug trafficking offence.
enrichment.outcome: 15-year travel restriction order quashed and replaced with a five-year order; the court gave general guidance on exercising section 33.
enrichment.ratio: A travel restriction order must be proportionate, tailored to assessed risk of reoffending after release, and supported by succinct reasons; importation alone does not automatically justify an order, and length should reflect age, pattern of travel, offence sophistication, and section 35 suspension provisions.
legal_issues: Purpose and proportionality of travel restriction orders under section 33
Factors relevant to the length of a travel restriction order
Whether reasons must be given for imposing an order and selecting its duration
Application of section 35 revocation and suspension regime

confidence.notes: Guidance and outcome on the specific order are clear; the judgment expressly notes the absence of prior reported authority.

notes: Extradition committal habeas corpus challenge on US disclosure refused; section 78 and Article 5 analysis is detailed.

enrichment.short_title: Extradition committal and disclosure to USA
key_facts: Wellington, a Jamaican national, was sought by the United States for two murders and related offences arising from a 1997 Kansas City shooting identified principally by co-accused Alonda Daniels.
He was provisionally arrested in January 2003 and committed after the district judge refused adjournment for further US disclosure, including statements from witnesses who allegedly exculpated him.
The applicant argued for prosecution-style disclosure, exclusion of Daniels' evidence under section 78 PACE, and abuse of process; the US maintained no such duty applied to fugitives.
District Judge Pratt found no bad faith or breach of candour and held the evidence sufficient to warrant committal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for habeas corpus following committal for extradition to the United States under the pre-2003 extradition regime.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: In extradition committal proceedings the requesting state chooses the evidence relied on and owes no general domestic prosecution disclosure duty absent bad faith or abuse; it must disclose material that would render relied evidence worthless, and section 78 PACE either does not apply or affords very limited scope in extradition.
legal_issues: Whether the requesting state has a duty of disclosure in extradition committal proceedings
Application of section 78 PACE 1984 to extradition proceedings
Scope of Article 5(4) ECHR adversarial requirements in extradition
Effect of Kashamu (No 1) on candour and fairness at committal
Whether Article IX(2) of the extradition treaty empowers the court to require further evidence
linked_authorities: R v Governor of Brixton Prison, ex parte Levin [1997] AC 714
R(Kashamu) v Governor of Brixton Prison (No 2) [2002] QB 887
R(Serbeh) v Governor of HMP Brixton [2002] EWHC Admin 2396
R v Governor of Pentonville Prison, Ex parte Lee [1993] 1 WLR 1294
Kirkwood v United Kingdom 6 EHRR 373

confidence.notes: Six propositions on extradition disclosure law and the dismissal outcome are clearly articulated, with a caveat on section 78 noted in the judgment.

notes: Firefighters' reinstatement after successful Secretary of State disciplinary appeal; regulation 18 Fire Service Regulations 1985 is central.

enrichment.short_title: Firefighters' reinstatement after Secretary of State appeal
key_facts: Four Hampshire firefighters were dismissed in 2001 after disciplinary proceedings for harassment, bullying and insubordination dating from the 1990s.
They appealed to the Secretary of State, who allowed the appeals in June 2003, substituting the dismissal decisions with effect from the original award dates under regulation 18.
Hampshire Fire and Rescue Service refused reinstatement in August 2003, maintaining dismissals were still effective and citing workforce morale and Article 8 concerns of other staff.
The claimants sought judicial review; one had reached retirement and sought amendment of his service record.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a fire authority's refusal to reinstate firefighters after a successful appeal to the Secretary of State under the Fire Service discipline regulations.
enrichment.outcome: Claims succeeded; reported dismissals declared void, August 2003 decisions quashed, mandatory reinstatement ordered with back pay and interest, and the third claimant's service record to be amended.
enrichment.ratio: Where misconduct falls within the Fire Service (Discipline) Regulations 1985, dismissal must follow that statutory scheme; regulation 18(2) substitutes the Secretary of State's decision for the original award, so the authority cannot refuse reinstatement or treat the disciplinary dismissal as continuing for a separate non-disciplinary reason.
legal_issues: Effect of regulation 18(2) substitution on continued employment status
Whether a fire authority may refuse reinstatement for operational or Article 8 reasons after a successful Secretary of State appeal
Justiciability of statutory disciplinary rights by judicial review
Whether unfair dismissal proceedings are an adequate alternative remedy
linked_authorities: R v Berkshire Health Authority ex parte Walsh [1984] 3 WLR 818
R v Derbyshire County Court ex parte Noble [1990] ICR 808
Abernethy v Mott, Hay and Anderson [1974] IRLR 213

confidence.notes: Statutory interpretation, relief, and costs are all clearly resolved with no dispute on final remedies.

notes: Litigant-in-person PHI quantum appeal dismissed; Lloyd's conceded a calculation error of £7,727.

enrichment.short_title: Lloyd's PHI damages quantum appeal dismissed
key_facts: Miss Healy sued Lloyd's for breach of contract in failing to provide permanent health insurance benefits after cervical spondylosis ended her secretarial employment in 1996.
Liability was admitted in April 2002; quantum turned on whether she could still work part-time until age 55, as rheumatologists indicated in May 2002 questionnaires.
Her solicitors came off the record days before the July 2002 quantum trial; she appeared in person, was refused an adjournment for updated medical evidence, and was awarded £148,418.
She obtained late evidence from Dr Walker in September 2002 that she was unfit for work, but the judge refused to admit it; Chadwick LJ granted permission on procedural fairness grounds.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against quantum assessment and case management decisions refusing adjournment and late medical evidence in a litigant-in-person damages trial.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Lloyd's conceded and offered an additional £7,727 to correct double-accounting of earnings and benefits in the judge's calculations.
enrichment.ratio: There was no procedural unfairness where the claimant chose to proceed in person, did not seek adjournment for legal representation, gave no indication she could not conduct her case, and the judge properly applied Ladd v Marshall to refuse late medical evidence after an adjournment had already been refused.
legal_issues: Whether refusal to adjourn for updated medical evidence was procedurally unfair
Whether the judge should have considered late medical evidence at judgment hand-down
Scope of permission to appeal where grounds shifted at hearing
Correct deduction for notional earnings versus benefits in PHI loss calculation
linked_authorities: Ladd v Marshall [1954] 1 WLR 1489

confidence.notes: Appeal grounds, withdrawal of adjournment complaint, and dismissal are explicit; the conceded calculation error is separately identified.

notes: SENDIST appeal on dyslexic pupil placement; tribunal erred in preferring coordinator evidence over psychologists.

enrichment.short_title: SEN tribunal error on dyslexic pupil placement
key_facts: L, a 14-year-old with dyslexia and a statement of special educational needs, struggled at mainstream secondary school after transfer in 2001.

Educational psychologist reports consistently showed a widening gap between her chronological age and reading, spelling and numeracy levels, indicating significant underachievement relative to average ability.
The SENDIST upheld the local authority's mainstream placement, preferring the SEN coordinator's optimistic school reports over the psychologists' evidence.
L's mother sought placement at a named residential school with dyslexia provision; the tribunal also relied on irrelevant comparisons with less able pupils.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal on a point of law against a Special Educational Needs and Disability Tribunal decision upholding mainstream school placement.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; decision quashed and matter remitted to a differently constituted tribunal; costs ordered against the local education authority.
enrichment.ratio: A tribunal may reject expert educational psychologist evidence only if supported by valid reasons and proper evidence; commendations for attitude and sport, and comparisons with less able statemented pupils, cannot rationally displace consistent underachievement data when deciding whether special educational needs are being met.
legal_issues: Standard of reasons required to reject expert educational psychologist evidence
Whether teacher optimism and attitude commendations can outweigh achievement-gap evidence
Relevance of comparing a pupil with less able statemented peers
Scope of the High Court's power to remit rather than direct residential placement

confidence.notes: Two clear errors of law are identified and the remittal order is explicit; the court did not predetermine the residential placement outcome.

notes: Special constitution custody time limit guidance; Bagoutie construction and resource availability affirmed.

enrichment.short_title: Custody time limit extension for murder trial

statutes_considered.title: Prosecution of Offences (Custody Time Limits) Regulations 1987
Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994

key_facts: Leslie and David Gibson were charged with murder in May 2003 and remained in custody; no body had been found and the trial required a High Court judge.

Judge Brodrick extended the 182-day custody time limit by 211 days to 10 June 2004 because Court 1 at Winchester was occupied by a transferred fraud trial and listing pressures included 30 outstanding murders.
The judge found the prosecution lacked due diligence in one minor respect but that failure had no causative effect on the need for extension.
The extension doubled the statutory limit plus one month, in a case listed for trial on 9 June 2004.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a Crown Court decision extending custody time limits before trial for murder.
enrichment.outcome: Applications dismissed; the court affirmed Bagoutie on linked due-diligence causation and held unavailability of a suitable High Court judge and courtroom could be good and sufficient cause for extension.
enrichment.ratio: Section 22(3) requires both good and sufficient cause and due diligence, but prosecution delay is fatal only if it caused the need for extension; limited court resources may justify extension where rigorously assessed, though routine listing difficulties must not emasculate custody time limits.
legal_issues: Whether lack of due diligence without causative effect prevents extension under section 22(3)
Whether unavailability of judges and courtrooms is good and sufficient cause
Intensity of judicial review where Article 5 rights are engaged
Appropriate length of extension where statutory limit is substantially exceeded
linked_authorities: R v Manchester Crown Court, ex parte McDonald [1999] 1 WLR 841
R v Leeds Crown Court, ex parte Bagoutie [1999] EWHC Admin 454
R(Bannister) v Crown Court at Guildford [2004] EWHC 221 Admin
R v Central Criminal Court, ex parte Abdu-Wardeh [1998] 1 WLR 1083
R v Central Criminal Court, ex parte Bennett (21 December 1998)

confidence.notes: Four issues are systematically addressed by a specially constituted court; outcome and guiding principles are clear despite policy concern about long extensions.

notes: Newham homelessness policy challenge; appeal allowed on viewing policy but unfair terms point upheld below.

enrichment.short_title: Newham homelessness offer policy and unfair terms

statutes_considered.title: Unfair Terms in Consumer Contracts Regulations 1999

key_facts: Three homeless applicants challenged Newham's policy requiring immediate acceptance or refusal of offered private sector leasing accommodation without prior viewing.
Under the policy, refusal could lead to instant cancellation of bed and breakfast accommodation; Newman J held the policy unlawful as contrary to guidance and procedurally unfair.
The Council argued the Part VII scheme gave no free-standing right to view property and that pressure to accept offers was necessary to move families out of bed and breakfast quickly.
Ms Khatun also argued that the Unfair Terms in Consumer Contracts Regulations 1999 applied to the tenancy terms offered under Part VII.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against judicial review granting relief to homeless applicants challenging a local authority housing allocation policy and tenancy terms.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part on the viewing policy; judge upheld on the second issue that the 1999 Regulations and Directive apply to Part VII tenancies offered by the council.
enrichment.ratio: Part VII of the Housing Act 1996 does not confer a right to view offered accommodation before deciding, and requiring immediate acceptance on pain of losing bed and breakfast is not oppressive where review and appeal rights remain; however the Unfair Terms Regulations apply to land contracts with public authorities acting in trade, business or profession.
legal_issues: Whether homeless applicants have a right to view accommodation before accepting a Part VII offer
Whether instant cancellation of bed and breakfast for refusal is Wednesbury irrational or disproportionate
Effect of statutory homelessness guidance under section 182
Whether Directive 93/13/EEC and the 1999 Regulations apply to public authority housing tenancies
linked_authorities: R v Secretary of State ex p. Shelter
R v North Derbyshire Health Authority ex p. Fisher
Cooper v Wandsworth Board of Works (1863) 14 CBNS 180

confidence.notes: Long judgment but first and second issues are clearly resolved with distinct outcomes; some criticism of respondents' solicitors noted but not outcome-determinative.

notes: Section 5A Sex Offenders Act restraining order upheld in principle but narrowed; viewing indecent images can cause serious psychological harm.

enrichment.short_title: Sex offender restraining order on indecent images
key_facts: Beaney pleaded guilty to 17 counts of making indecent photographs of children after police found cached browser images on his computer, including level 4 and 5 material.
He was sentenced to six months' imprisonment, forfeiture of his computer, and an indefinite restraining order banning ownership or access to internet-capable and image-viewing equipment.
A psychologist assessed low risk of contact offences but medium risk of reoffending by downloading; the judge gave no explicit reasons for the restraining order.
The court considered Halloren on the necessity and serious harm requirements of section 5A(2).
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for leave to appeal against a section 5A Sex Offenders Act restraining order imposed on sentence.
enrichment.outcome: Leave granted and appeal allowed in part; restraining order varied to remove 'access to' wording and narrow equipment definitions while otherwise upheld.
enrichment.ratio: A section 5A restraining order requires necessity to protect the public or particular members from serious harm; viewing indecent images can contribute to the serious psychological harm suffered by depicted children, so such an order may be justified even where contact-offence risk is low, but terms must not exceed what is necessary.
legal_issues: Meaning of serious harm under section 5A(2) Sex Offenders Act 1997
Whether downloading and viewing indecent images creates harm to depicted children
Appropriate breadth of equipment restrictions in a restraining order
Application of Halloren to orders lacking explicit reasons
linked_authorities: Halloren [2004] EWCA Crim 233
Oliver [2003] 2 Cr App R(S) 15

confidence.notes: Legal test and specific order variations are clearly stated; the judgment develops the harm rationale for non-contact image offences.

notes: Short CCRC reference on unlawful licence recall backdating under section 116 PCC(S)A 2000.

key_facts: The appellant was sentenced in April 2001 to two and a half years for theft and breach of licence, released on licence in June 2002 with 386 days remaining.
His licence was revoked on 8 August 2002 after an assault; he later escaped and received consecutive sentences for ABH and escape.
The Recorder ordered the 386-day balance to run from 8 August 2002, but section 116(2)(a) required the period to begin only on the date of the court order.
The Court of Appeal had already reduced the escape sentence to 15 months consecutive; the prison authorities could not give effect to the Recorder's backdating.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Reference by the Criminal Cases Review Commission on the lawfulness of the period specified for serving a revoked licence.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed to the extent indicated; 386 days substituted with 58 days for the short-term prisoner to reflect lawful commencement under section 116(2)(a).
enrichment.ratio: Under section 116(2)(a) of the Powers of Criminal Courts (Sentencing) Act 2000, a period of imprisonment imposed on licence revocation can only begin on the date of the court's order, not from the earlier date of licence revocation, even where the sentencing judge clearly intended backdating.
legal_issues: Construction of section 116(2)(a) PCC(S)A 2000 on commencement of licence recall periods
Whether a court may order licence balance to run from the date of revocation
Adjustment for short-term prisoner status and time unlawfully at large

confidence.notes: Short judgment but the statutory point and substituted period are explicit; factual detail is minimal by design.
